outcome: John Pardon proved the MNOP conjecture (the Gromov-Witten/Donaldson-Thomas correspondence) for all complex threefolds with nef anti-canonical bundle, including all Calabi-Yau threefolds, with primary insertions, in a preprint first posted 5 August 2023 (arXiv:2308.02948) — before the frozen revision's 26 January 2024 cutoff. The proof has since received full expert digestion and top-tier recognition within the window: the 2025 Breakthrough Prize New Horizons in Mathematics Prize (announced April 2025) and, more decisively, the 2026 Fields Medal (announced 23 July 2026), whose IMU citation credits Pardon's work including this proof.
summary: The mathematical event that settles this problem — Pardon's proof that curve-enumeration invariants of complex threefolds with nef anti-canonical bundle (in particular all Calabi-Yau threefolds) are determined by their values on local curves, which combined with the known MNOP correspondence for local curves (Bryan-Okounkov-Pandharipande) establishes the MNOP conjecture with primary insertions for this class — was first posted to arXiv as v1 of arXiv:2308.02948 on 5 August 2023, before the frozen revision's 26 January 2024 cutoff. Per §6.3 this is the date that governs, and per §6.1 that makes the underlying result 'settled before the frozen revision's date' — hence open_stale, recorded but not counted as an in-window change. However, the expert digestion that would distinguish 'claimed' from 'resolved' (per §6.1: an expert digestion that works through the proof, or equivalent recognition by named experts) accumulated substantially within the window: a v2 revision (14 February 2024, ~24% larger, suggesting nontrivial elaboration though I could not access a changelog), the 2025 Breakthrough Prize New Horizons in Mathematics Prize citing this specific proof (announced April 2025), and — most decisively — the 2026 Fields Medal (announced 23 July 2026 at the ICM in Philadelphia), whose citation and the accompanying Quanta Magazine profile credit Pardon's MNOP proof as a central achievement, with mathematicians quoted describing the novel 'Pardon algebra' apparatus of the proof. No source anywhere — the arXiv abstract/paper, the Quanta profile, the prize announcements, or the Wikipedia biography of Pardon — mentions any AI or machine-learning system in connection with this proof; it is entirely human-derived, hand-written mathematics using a new structure Pardon built (generic transversality for complex structures, following and adapting Ionel-Parker's approach to the Gopakumar-Vafa conjecture). I classified as open_stale rather than resolved because the rule dates by the first written argument, and that argument predates the freeze; the extensive in-window recognition is real but is digestion of a pre-existing result, not a new mathematical event.
competing_reading: A strong case exists for `resolved` instead of `open_stale`: the wording of §6.1 ties `resolved` to whether 'a human expert has read the argument' and treats a full expert digestion as the operative event distinguishing it from a mere unverified `claimed` preprint. That digestion — full peer engagement, the 2025 Breakthrough Prize, and above all the 2026 Fields Medal citation explicitly crediting this proof — is concentrated inside the window, even though the original preprint (and the mathematical content of the proof) predates it. If the intended reading of `open_stale` is narrower (limited to cases where a problem was already fully resolved and settled by consensus before the freeze, with no further in-window development), then this problem does not fit that narrower reading, since as of January 2024 the proof was a very recent (5-month-old) unrefereed preprint, not yet digested, and the digestion event (which is what converts status from `claimed` to `resolved`) happened afterward. Under that reading the correct status would be `resolved`, dated to the Fields Medal citation (23 July 2026) or the 2025 Breakthrough Prize (April 2025), as an announcement/press event marking expert consensus, with `predates_frozen_revision` false.
what_would_settle_it: A clarification of whether §6.3's 'first public written argument' rule is meant to override §6.1's resolved/claimed distinction when the two events (initial preprint vs. expert digestion) straddle the freeze date — i.e., whether 'open_stale' is reserved strictly for results whose entire lifecycle (proof and consensus) predates the freeze, or whether it applies whenever the first written argument predates the freeze regardless of when consensus formed.
